title: AI agents explained: What they are and how they work
gist: Meta's technical explainer lays out AI agents as LLM-cored systems built from four architectural components (LLM reasoning core, persistent memory, planning/task breakdown, and tool/API connectivity) running in a continuous perceive-act-evaluate loop, proposes a four-type agent taxonomy (reactive, goal-based, utility-based, learning) and a three-tier bots-versus-assistants-versus-agents capability ladder, and cites BLS/PwC figures sizing the addressable household-time-savings opportunity.

insights.claim: Meta defines an AI agent's architecture around four components: an LLM core that serves as the central reasoning/processing engine and supports step-by-step decision-making, memory that persists both within-conversation context and longer-term saved preferences across sessions, planning that breaks a goal into sequenced sub-steps and compares options against criteria, and tool/API connectivity that lets the agent update data or trigger actions in external systems.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This four-component architecture is a concrete technical checklist for evaluating whether a product marketed as an 'AI agent' actually has the necessary building blocks (versus being a scripted assistant).
insights.locator: How AI agents work under a user's direction

insights.claim: The underlying operating mechanism is described as a continuous loop: the agent receives input, processes it, performs an action, evaluates the result, and adjusts if needed — the cycle that enables autonomous multi-step operation from a single initial prompt.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This perceive-act-evaluate loop is the mechanistic explanation for how agents sustain multi-step autonomy, useful for technically assessing agent product claims.
insights.locator: Tools, APIs, and the ability to take action

insights.claim: The AI agent systems users are likely to interact with are typically composed of sub-agents, allowing the overall system to work on different parts of a goal simultaneously, or even pursue different goals at the same time.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: Confirms multi-agent orchestration (sub-agents working in parallel) is the production architecture pattern behind consumer-facing 'single agent' products, relevant to understanding the actual engineering complexity behind agent UX.
insights.locator: AI agent systems composed of sub-agents

themes.theme: A four-type taxonomy of agent behavior

insights.claim: Meta proposes four agent-type design patterns rather than mutually exclusive categories: reactive agents that respond to live conditions (e.g., flagging an unusual account charge the moment it appears), goal-based agents that measure every decision against a single anchor goal (e.g., a ten-week half-marathon training plan), utility-based agents that optimize for the best outcome among tradeoffs rather than merely reaching a goal (e.g., selecting patio plants for partial sun and butterflies), and learning agents that adapt behavior over time from feedback (e.g., detecting a migraine trigger pattern from logged entries).
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This four-type taxonomy gives a concrete framework for classifying and comparing different AI agent products by their underlying decision logic rather than by marketing claims.

themes.theme: Capability ladder: bots vs. assistants vs. agents

insights.claim: Meta lays out a three-tier capability ladder: bots follow fixed rules with low capability (e.g., FAQ bots, spam filters) and are best for simple repetitive tasks; prompt-based AI assistants respond to prompts with medium capability and help complete tasks step by step (e.g., search, draft, summarize); AI agents achieve user-set goals with high capability by breaking tasks into steps and executing them (e.g., handling a full product return — order lookup, policy check, label generation, pickup scheduling — under user oversight).
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This is Meta's own market-segmentation framework distinguishing bots, assistants, and agents by capability tier, useful for positioning competitor products (or Meta's own) within this ladder.
insights.quote: bots follow rules, assistants follow instructions, and agents execute toward goals.
insights.locator: Key difference: Agentic vs. non-agentic systems

insights.claim: Because agents take real actions rather than only generating text, Meta states that errors in agent workflows can have more tangible real-world consequences than a wrong answer from a chatbot.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This elevates the stakes of the reliability problem for agents compared to chatbots, directly relevant to how much autonomy users and regulators should be comfortable granting current-generation agent products.
insights.locator: Understanding the limitations: risks and responsible use

insights.claim: Citing US Bureau of Labor Statistics data, Meta states Americans spend over two hours a day on household tasks alone, before factoring in shopping and other personal admin, and cites a PwC estimate that AI-enabled household support could deliver up to $330 billion in socioeconomic value.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: The $330 billion socioeconomic-value estimate is a specific market-sizing figure for the AI-enabled household-support opportunity that could be used to benchmark agentic-AI market TAM claims.
insights.locator: Get time back on everyday tasks

insights.claim: Meta frames agent security as permission-scoped: an agent can only reach the accounts and apps a user has explicitly connected, and recommends starting with only the connections needed for the task at hand and periodically removing unused access.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This is Meta's stated access-control model for agent products, relevant to assessing the attack surface and data-exposure risk of connected-agent ecosystems.

themes.theme: Trajectory: from bots to assistants to agents

insights.claim: Meta frames current agentic products — meeting-prep tools that pull context from scattered emails and files, apps that log a meal from a single photo, and systems that draft a dispute letter when an unauthorized charge appears — as 'early examples' of agentic behavior, predicting these will expand into more complex multi-step consumer workflows such as adaptive training plans, migraine-pattern detection, and savings-goal tracking as the technology matures.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: This is Meta's own forward-looking product roadmap signal for where consumer agentic AI features are headed next, useful for anticipating Meta's future AI product launches.
insights.locator: How AI agents change the way everyday tasks get done

insights.claim: Meta states the progression from chatbots to assistants to agents reflects a broader shift from 'AI that responds' to 'AI that executes,' and predicts the line between tools that help people think and tools that help them get things done will continue to narrow as agent technology matures.
insights.speaker: Meta AI Blog
insights.so_what: Articulates Meta's thesis on the long-term trajectory of consumer AI products, useful context for evaluating whether future Meta AI features will increasingly default to agentic, action-taking behavior rather than purely conversational responses.
